The proposed metasurface is composed of two different non-resonant unit cells (MAMC1 and MAMC2) arranged in a chessboard-like pattern.
The non-resonant unit cells are made of stacked non-resonant patches separated by thin dielectric substrates.
The 10-dB RCSR bandwidth of the ideal metasurface design was 150%, from 5.37 GHz to 37.5 GHz.
The 10-dB RCSR bandwidth of the ROGERS metasurface design was 133%, from 6.37 GHz to 31.72 GHz.
The 10-dB RCSR bandwidth of the low-cost metasurface design using FR-4 substrate was 141%, from 4.89 GHz to 28.37 GHz.
The fabricated low-cost metasurface demonstrated a 10-dB RCSR bandwidth from 5.22 GHz to 30.85 GHz, corresponding to a 142% fractional bandwidth.
The low-cost metasurface had a simple and lightweight structure, with each unit cell composed of 0.5 mm FR-4 substrates and air gap spacers.
The 10-dB RCSR bandwidth of the low-cost metasurface was more than 98% for TM-polarization and more than 51% for TE-polarization up to 40 degrees oblique incidence angles.

The authors used a genetic algorithm (GA) to optimize the unit cell design parameters, including patch lengths, substrate thicknesses, and dielectric constants, to achieve the widest possible 180° ± 37° phase difference bandwidth.

The non-resonant behavior of the unit cells provided more linearity in the reflection phase response versus frequency, enabling wider 180° ± 37° destructive reflection phase cancellation compared to resonant unit cells.
The proposed metasurface exhibited significantly wider RCSR bandwidth compared to the state-of-the-art references, which typically achieved 10-dB RCSR bandwidths in the range of 70-126%.

The authors modeled the non-resonant unit cell using an equivalent circuit consisting of parallel capacitors and transmission lines, which allowed them to calculate the effective capacitance and input impedance of the unit cell.
The chessboard-like arrangement of the two different unit cells (MAMC1 and MAMC2) created destructive interference and minimized the monostatic RCS at normal incidence.
The 3D scattering patterns of the proposed metasurface showed four main lobes and zeros in the incident direction, due to the phase cancellation between adjacent tiles.
The low-cost availability, simple structure, and wide RCSR bandwidth of the proposed metasurface make it a promising candidate for practical applications.
